screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what separates tests that help development from tests that slow it down. Good tests provide rapid feedback, isolate behavior, and remain useful as code evolves. We will use the FIRST principles — Fast, Isolated, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely — as a checklist for quality, and the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern to structure each test clearly. You will see concrete examples that compare brittle tests to well-factored ones, and a short refactoring exercise that replaces a shared repository with isolated mocks. Understanding these ideas matters because a healthy test suite enables safe refactoring, catches regressions early, and keeps developer confidence high. A common trap is creating tests that are slow or dependent on external state; we'll show pragmatic fixes like mocking and scoped fixtures. By the end of this chapter you will be able to evaluate tests for FIRST compliance, rewrite tests to follow AAA, and identify brittle or overly broad tests. Consider the test suite as part of your design — test quality is design quality. What test in your project would you examine first to apply these principles?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Overview
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Writing Good Tests: Characteristics and Best Practices

This chapter teaches how to write unit tests that are easy to run, diagnose, and maintain. We'll use FIRST and AAA as practical rules to make your test suite an asset rather than a liability.

In this lesson
Identify the FIRST principles and structure tests with AAA.
Coming up
Refactor a shared-test example into isolated unit tests using mocks.
Why it matters
Fast, reliable tests let you change code confidently and ship safely.
Explore Key Topics
FIRST principles
Fast, Isolated, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely
Arrange-Act-Assert
Structure every test for clarity
Mocking & Fixtures
Replace slow dependencies for speed and isolation
Concept map
FIRST → AAA → Maintainability
Fast: keep tests small and avoid external IO
Isolated: use mocks or fresh fixtures
Timely: write tests before or alongside code
Quick start

We will inspect bad tests that use a shared repository, then refactor them into small, focused tests that use a mock repository. Follow the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern as a habit.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the characteristics of a good unit test and apply practical techniques to improve tests. First, you will recognize the FIRST principles and explain why they matter for speed and reliability. Second, you will structure test code using the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern so each test has a single clear purpose. Third, you'll spot and fix common pitfalls such as brittle tests, overly broad tests, and tests that leak state between runs. Finally, you will refactor tests to use mocks or fresh fixtures so they run quickly and consistently in local and CI environments. Each objective is paired with a short practice step: inspect an existing test, refactor setup to be isolated, replace a real repository with a mock, and split a broad test into smaller focused tests. These are practical skills that directly reduce developer friction and increase confidence during refactoring. Think about a slow or flaky test you know — you'll apply these skills to that example after this chapter.

screens.title: FIRST Principles: Overview
screens.narratorSegment: FIRST is a compact checklist that helps you evaluate whether a unit test will be useful day to day. Fast means tests execute quickly so developers run them often; slow tests discourage frequent runs and hide regressions. Isolated means each test runs independently; it should not rely on the execution order or shared state. Repeatable means running the same test produces the same outcome across machines and environments; avoid depending on external services or unseeded randomness. Self-validating means the test returns a clear boolean result — you should not need to inspect logs or manual output to know if it passed. Timely means tests are written before or alongside the code they validate, which helps tests drive design and keeps test coverage meaningful. A concrete example: if a registration test talks to a real database it may be slow and non-repeatable; replacing that dependency with a mock makes the test fast and isolated. A common misconception is that more assertions equal better tests; in fact, packing many concerns into a single test makes it hard to diagnose failures and violates isolation. As a takeaway, use FIRST as a living checklist when you write or refactor tests, and ask: would this test still be valuable after refactors?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › FIRST Principles
Definition

FIRST is an acronym for five desirable properties of unit tests. It is a quick evaluation tool when inspecting or writing tests.

Fast — avoid IO and long setup
Isolated — no cross-test dependencies
Repeatable — deterministic across environments
Self-validating — clear pass/fail via assertions
Timely — write tests as part of development
Example & Misconception
Example: A registration test that touches a real database is slow and tied to external state. Replace the database with a mock to make it fast and isolated. Misconception: Adding more checks inside one test makes it better. In reality, multiple assertions on unrelated behavior hide the true cause of failure. Prefer separate tests that each assert one behavior.
Key Takeaway

Apply FIRST as a short review for tests. If a test fails this checklist, prioritize refactoring for reliability and speed.

screens.title: Fast: Keep Unit Tests Quick
screens.narratorSegment: Fast tests enable a tight development loop. When unit tests run in seconds, developers run them frequently, catching regressions immediately. The common cause of slow tests is external input and output: real databases, file systems, or network calls. Another cause is a heavy shared fixture that does unnecessary setup for every test. A practical fix is to replace slow dependencies with lightweight mocks or in-memory doubles, and to scope fixtures tightly. For example, the bad test example uses a module-scoped repository that connects to a database; it slows every test and can leak state across tests. Switching to a function-scoped mock ensures each test runs in isolation and completes quickly. A typical misconception is that integration with a real database always yields better confidence. While integration tests are important, they should live in a separate, slower suite — unit tests must stay quick. As a takeaway, measure test runtime and prioritize turning the slowest unit tests into isolated, mocked tests. One question to consider: if a failing test takes a minute to run, how likely are you to run it while iterating?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Fast Tests
Problem

Slow tests discourage frequent runs and hide regressions. They are often caused by real database or network access and broad shared setup.

Measure runtime and identify slow tests.
Replace external IO with mocks or in-memory fakes.
Use function-scoped fixtures to avoid expensive shared setup.
Concrete example
The bad test used a module-scoped ProductRepository that connects to a real database. That setup runs once but can be slow and leak state. Instead, provide a fresh mock repository for each test using unittest.mock.Mock so each test is fast and deterministic.
Key Takeaway

Prioritize speed: if a unit test is slow, refactor its dependencies into mocks or narrower fixtures.

screens.title: Isolated Tests and Fixture Scope
screens.narratorSegment: Isolation means a test does not depend on or change the state used by other tests. If tests are order-dependent or share mutable fixtures, failures cascade and debugging becomes painful. A common pattern that breaks isolation is a session- or module-scoped fixture that reuses one repository instance across many tests. That shared state can hide inter-test dependencies and lead to brittle results. The recommended approach is to use fresh test doubles or function-scoped fixtures so each test begins from a known state. For example, replace a shared ProductRepository fixture with a mock created for each test using unittest. mock. Mock. This preserves the interactions you want to verify while preventing state leakage. A misconception is believing that fewer fixtures reduce maintenance; in reality, tightly-scoped fixtures reduce hidden coupling and make tests easier to reason about. As a practical rule: when a test needs setup, make that setup local to the test or explicitly reset state in a teardown step. Which setup would you prefer for long-term maintainability — a single shared object you must reason about across tests, or a fresh, predictable object per test?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Isolation
Comparison: Shared vs Per-test
Shared fixture (module/session scope): faster setup but risks leaked state and order dependence.
Per-test mock: slightly more setup but gives isolation and predictable behavior.
Concrete guidance
  • Create mocks inside fixtures with function scope or directly in the test.
  • Reset or recreate any stateful object between tests.
  • Use assert_called_once_with to verify behavior rather than inspecting repository internals.
Common mistake

Reusing a repository object across many tests can hide coupling and produce intermittent failures. Prefer fresh doubles for clarity.

screens.title: Repeatable and Self-Validating Tests
screens.narratorSegment: Repeatable tests give the same result regardless of where or when they run. To achieve repeatability avoid unseeded randomness, machine-specific dates, or network-dependent resources. If a test needs pseudo-random data, seed the generator inside the test so the sequence is deterministic. Self-validating tests make pass/fail explicit by using assertions; a test should not require manual inspection. Assertions should check behavior or contract — for example, an operation returns True or an object has the expected state — rather than relying on print statements or visual checks. The bad UserService example mixes registration and retrieval and relies on a database; that makes the test non-isolated and risks non-repeatability. The improved example uses a mock repository and explicit assertions on return values and interactions, such as assert_called_once_with to validate expected behavior. A common misconception is that logging or prints are sufficient for validation; logs are useful for debugging but not for automated verification. The takeaway: make every test deterministic and assert its outcome so CI can trust the result. Which external factor in your tests could make results fluctuate? Repeatable and Self-Validating Tests means ensure tests always produce the same result and use assertions that explicitly state expected outcomes, not manual checks.. In practical terms, deterministic outcomes and explicit assertions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Repeatable & Self-validating
Repeatable rules
Avoid reliance on system time, network, or unseeded randomness. If randomness is required, seed it inside the test. Use deterministic fixtures and mocks so tests behave identically across machines.
Seed random generators in tests when needed.
Avoid external network calls; stub or mock them.
Self-validating checks

Use assertions to express expected outcomes. For behavioral verification, assert return values and interactions with mocks instead of reading logs or relying on side effects alone.

Key Takeaway

Every test should deterministically produce a pass or fail signal that CI can interpret without human review.

screens.title: Timely: Tests Drive Design
screens.narratorSegment: Timely tests are written before or alongside the production code, as in test-driven development. Writing tests first clarifies the public interface, forces you to think about edge cases, and keeps design focused on observable behavior. When tests are added after the fact, they often mirror implementation details and become brittle when the implementation changes. A short example: writing a test for a register_user function first makes you define what success should look like — a boolean result and a call to the repository — which keeps the service's interface minimal and testable. A misconception is that TDD adds overhead; in practice it reduces rework by catching design issues early. The takeaway is to treat tests as part of design: when possible, create a failing test that describes the expected behavior, implement the minimal code to pass it, and then refactor both code and tests together. How might writing a test first change the way you design a new service method? Timely: Tests Drive Design means writing tests early clarifies interfaces, encourages small apis, and reduces brittle coupling to implementation details.. In practical terms, write tests before the production code to guide design. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Timely / TDD
Why write tests first?

Tests written before code force you to specify behavior and edge cases. They serve as an executable specification and keep APIs small and testable.

Write a failing test that describes desired behavior.
Implement the minimal code to satisfy the test.
Refactor code and tests, keeping behavior intact.
Practical tip

If you find tests are tightly coupled to internals, consider refactoring the implementation or the test: either the behavior should be surfaced or the test should be adapted to verify contracts rather than internals.

Misconception

TDD is not just slower upfront; it prevents larger rework by keeping intent explicit and tests stable as design evolves.

screens.title: Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA)
screens.narratorSegment: Arrange-Act-Assert is a simple but powerful structure for each unit test. Arrange sets up inputs, objects, and mocks; Act executes the behavior under test; Assert verifies the outcome. Using AAA helps ensure each test has one clear reason to fail and makes failures easy to diagnose. A concrete example from the good UserService tests: Arrange creates a fresh mock repository and a user service instance; Act calls register_user with test credentials; Assert checks the returned result and verifies the repository interaction with assert_called_once_with. A frequent mistake is mixing multiple actions in one test — for instance, testing registration and retrieval together. That violates the single-responsibility rule and makes failures ambiguous. Another misconception is that setting up everything in fixtures hides complexity; move setup into Arrange when it is specific to a single test. The takeaway: structure tests explicitly with AAA and keep each test focused on a single behavior. What would you extract into Arrange for a complex scenario? Arrange-Act-Assert (AAA) means arrange inputs, act on the system, and assert the observable behavior so each test has one clear purpose.. In practical terms, a disciplined test structure for clarity and single-purpose tests. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Arrange-Act-Assert
AAA pattern
Arrange: create fresh mocks and inputs. Act: perform a single behavior. Assert: check results and interactions. Keep each test focused to one behavior.
Arrange: mock_user_repository = Mock()
Act: result = user_service.register_user(username, password)
Assert: assert result is True and repository.add called once
Example test snippet
# Arrange
mock_repo = Mock()
user_service = UserService(mock_repo)
username = "bob"
password = "secure_password"

# Act
result = user_service.register_user(username, password)

# Assert
assert result is True
mock_repo.add.assert_called_once_with({"username": username, "password": password})
Key Takeaway

Write tests so Arrange, Act, and Assert are explicit and each test has one reason to fail.

screens.title: Bad vs Good Tests: UserService Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare two tests to see how FIRST and AAA are applied. The bad example uses a UserService connected to a real database via a module-scoped fixture. It registers a user and then retrieves it in the same test, which mixes responsibilities and depends on external state. This violates Fast, Isolated, and Self-validating principles because the database makes the test slow, shared fixtures lead to order dependence, and multiple behaviors hide the true failure source. The good example uses unittest. mock. Mock for the repository and splits scenarios into separate tests that follow Arrange-Act-Assert. Each test focuses on one outcome: successful registration or duplicate registration. The tests assert return values and interactions with the mock, using assert_called_once_with and return_value setups on the mock. A common misconception is that integration with a real backend always gives better coverage; integration tests are important, but they belong in a separate suite. As a learner, when you see a lifecycle test, ask whether it can be split into focused tests with mocks. Which part of the original lifecycle test would you extract first? Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Bad vs Good
Bad test (excerpt)
import pytest
from user_service import UserService

@pytest.fixture(scope="module")
def user_service_with_db():
    service = UserService(database_connection_string="real_db_prod")
    service.clear_all_users()
    yield service
    service.clear_all_users()

def test_register_and_get_user(user_service_with_db):
    user_service_with_db.register_user("alice", "password123")
    user = user_service_with_db.get_user("alice")
    assert user.username == "alice"
    assert user.email is None
Problems: hits a real DB, mixes two behaviors, and uses a long-lived fixture that may affect other tests.
Good test (excerpt)
from unittest.mock import Mock

@pytest.fixture
def mock_user_repository():
    return Mock()

@pytest.fixture
def user_service(mock_user_repository):
    return UserService(mock_user_repository)

def test_register_user_success(user_service, mock_user_repository):
    username = "bob"
    password = "secure_password"

    result = user_service.register_user(username, password)

    assert result is True
    mock_user_repository.add.assert_called_once_with({"username": username, "password": password})
Improvement: uses a mock, isolates behavior, and asserts interactions explicitly.

screens.title: Brittle Tests and Overly Broad Tests
screens.narratorSegment: Brittle tests break for reasons unrelated to the intended behavior of the code. They usually assert implementation details such as exact error message text, internal data structures, or ordering that is not part of the contract. Overly broad tests bundle multiple behaviors into a single test so a single failure gives poor diagnostic information. To fix brittleness, assert observable behavior or types rather than exact strings. For example, assert that an error of a given type is raised instead of matching the full error message. To fix overly broad tests, split them into focused tests that each verify a single expectation. Another useful practice is to extract shared setup into helper functions only when it genuinely reduces duplication without hiding important context. A misconception is believing that asserting deeper internals tests more thoroughly; in truth it makes tests fragile when internals are refactored. The takeaway: tests should express intent and contract, not implementation details. Ask yourself, if I refactor the implementation but keep behavior the same, will this test still pass? Signs of brittle tests

screens.title: Mocking and Stubbing: When and How
screens.narratorSegment: Mocks and stubs are test doubles that let you isolate the code under test from slow or stateful dependencies. Use them to replace databases, external APIs, or heavy services during unit testing. A stub provides canned responses, while a mock also records interactions for verification. The product_service refactor in the hands-on activity shows replacing a shared ProductRepository with a Mock for each test and then asserting interactions like add. assert_called_once_with. Start by identifying dependencies in the service constructor and parameterize them so tests can inject doubles. Avoid overusing mocks: mock behavior that is external and irrelevant to the unit's logic, but keep core logic verified through return values and state. A misconception is to mock everything; that hides integration issues. Balance your suite: fast unit tests with mocks and a smaller set of integration tests for end-to-end confidence. As a practical step, create a mock fixture that returns a fresh Mock instance per test and use it both for behavioral assertions and for simulating error conditions. content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Mocking & Stubbing
When to mock
  • External services or databases that make tests slow or flaky.
  • Services whose failures you want to simulate deterministically.
  • Dependencies that are not under test but whose interactions matter.
How to mock
Dependency-inject a repository or client into your service, then in tests provide a fresh unittest.mock.Mock instance. Use return_value to simulate responses and assert_called_once_with to verify expected calls.
@pytest.fixture
def mock_product_repository():
    return Mock()

def test_create_product_success(mock_product_repository):
    service = ProductService(mock_product_repository)
    product_id = "P001"
    service.create_product(product_id, "Laptop", 1200.0)
    mock_product_repository.add.assert_called_once_with({"id": product_id, "name": "Laptop", "price": 1200.0})
Key Takeaway

Design for injection of dependencies so tests can supply mocks and stay fast and focused.

Starter refactor snippet
from unittest.mock import Mock
import pytest
from product_service import ProductService

@pytest.fixture
def mock_repository():
    return Mock()

@pytest.fixture
def product_service(mock_repository):
    return ProductService(mock_repository)

def test_create_product_success(product_service, mock_repository):
    # Arrange
    product_id = "P001"

    result = product_service.create_product(product_id, "Laptop", 1200.00)

    mock_repository.add.assert_called_once_with({"id": product_id, "name": "Laptop", "price": 1200.0})

Refactoring tests into small, mocked units improves speed and makes failures easier to act on.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what separates tests that help development from tests that slow it down. Good tests provide rapid feedback, isolate behavior, and remain useful as code evolves. We will use the FIRST principles — Fast, Isolated, Repeatable, Self-validating, Timely — as a checklist for quality, and the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern to structure each test clearly. You will see concrete examples that compare brittle tests to well-factored ones, and a short refactoring exercise that replaces a shared repository with isolated mocks. Understanding these ideas matters because a healthy test suite enables safe refactoring, catches regressions early, and keeps developer confidence high. A common trap is creating tests that are slow or dependent on external state; we'll show pragmatic fixes like mocking and scoped fixtures. By the end of this chapter you will be able to evaluate tests for FIRST compliance, rewrite tests to follow AAA, and identify brittle or overly broad tests. Consider the test suite as part of your design — test quality is design quality. What test in your project would you examine first to apply these principles?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify the characteristics of a good unit test and apply practical techniques to improve tests. First, you will recognize the FIRST principles and explain why they matter for speed and reliability. Second, you will structure test code using the Arrange-Act-Assert pattern so each test has a single clear purpose. Third, you'll spot and fix common pitfalls such as brittle tests, overly broad tests, and tests that leak state between runs. Finally, you will refactor tests to use mocks or fresh fixtures so they run quickly and consistently in local and CI environments. Each objective is paired with a short practice step: inspect an existing test, refactor setup to be isolated, replace a real repository with a mock, and split a broad test into smaller focused tests. These are practical skills that directly reduce developer friction and increase confidence during refactoring. Think about a slow or flaky test you know — you'll apply these skills to that example after this chapter.

This page lists four hands-on skills you'll practice as you work through the chapter. First, you will identify slow or stateful tests and convert their external dependencies into mocks or stubs, ensuring tests become fast and isolated. Second, you will refactor a large lifecycle test into multiple focused tests that follow Arrange-Act-Assert, making each test easier to reason about. Third, you will recognize brittle assertions and replace them with behavior-focused checks that tolerate harmless implementation changes. Fourth, you will adopt simple fixture scoping: prefer function-scoped fixtures or freshly created test doubles rather than long-lived shared fixtures that leak state. Each skill directly reduces false positives and developer friction. These tasks simulate the real-world work of keeping a test suite healthy and are small enough to complete in a short lab session. When you practice, measure time-to-run before and after, and notice how isolating dependencies directly improves both speed and confidence.

FIRST is a compact checklist that helps you evaluate whether a unit test will be useful day to day. Fast means tests execute quickly so developers run them often; slow tests discourage frequent runs and hide regressions. Isolated means each test runs independently; it should not rely on the execution order or shared state. Repeatable means running the same test produces the same outcome across machines and environments; avoid depending on external services or unseeded randomness. Self-validating means the test returns a clear boolean result — you should not need to inspect logs or manual output to know if it passed. Timely means tests are written before or alongside the code they validate, which helps tests drive design and keeps test coverage meaningful. A concrete example: if a registration test talks to a real database it may be slow and non-repeatable; replacing that dependency with a mock makes the test fast and isolated. A common misconception is that more assertions equal better tests; in fact, packing many concerns into a single test makes it hard to diagnose failures and violates isolation. As a takeaway, use FIRST as a living checklist when you write or refactor tests, and ask: would this test still be valuable after refactors?

Fast tests enable a tight development loop. When unit tests run in seconds, developers run them frequently, catching regressions immediately. The common cause of slow tests is external input and output: real databases, file systems, or network calls. Another cause is a heavy shared fixture that does unnecessary setup for every test. A practical fix is to replace slow dependencies with lightweight mocks or in-memory doubles, and to scope fixtures tightly. For example, the bad test example uses a module-scoped repository that connects to a database; it slows every test and can leak state across tests. Switching to a function-scoped mock ensures each test runs in isolation and completes quickly. A typical misconception is that integration with a real database always yields better confidence. While integration tests are important, they should live in a separate, slower suite — unit tests must stay quick. As a takeaway, measure test runtime and prioritize turning the slowest unit tests into isolated, mocked tests. One question to consider: if a failing test takes a minute to run, how likely are you to run it while iterating?

Isolation means a test does not depend on or change the state used by other tests. If tests are order-dependent or share mutable fixtures, failures cascade and debugging becomes painful. A common pattern that breaks isolation is a session- or module-scoped fixture that reuses one repository instance across many tests. That shared state can hide inter-test dependencies and lead to brittle results. The recommended approach is to use fresh test doubles or function-scoped fixtures so each test begins from a known state. For example, replace a shared ProductRepository fixture with a mock created for each test using unittest. mock. Mock. This preserves the interactions you want to verify while preventing state leakage. A misconception is believing that fewer fixtures reduce maintenance; in reality, tightly-scoped fixtures reduce hidden coupling and make tests easier to reason about. As a practical rule: when a test needs setup, make that setup local to the test or explicitly reset state in a teardown step. Which setup would you prefer for long-term maintainability — a single shared object you must reason about across tests, or a fresh, predictable object per test?

Repeatable tests give the same result regardless of where or when they run. To achieve repeatability avoid unseeded randomness, machine-specific dates, or network-dependent resources. If a test needs pseudo-random data, seed the generator inside the test so the sequence is deterministic. Self-validating tests make pass/fail explicit by using assertions; a test should not require manual inspection. Assertions should check behavior or contract — for example, an operation returns True or an object has the expected state — rather than relying on print statements or visual checks. The bad UserService example mixes registration and retrieval and relies on a database; that makes the test non-isolated and risks non-repeatability. The improved example uses a mock repository and explicit assertions on return values and interactions, such as assert_called_once_with to validate expected behavior. A common misconception is that logging or prints are sufficient for validation; logs are useful for debugging but not for automated verification. The takeaway: make every test deterministic and assert its outcome so CI can trust the result. Which external factor in your tests could make results fluctuate? Repeatable and Self-Validating Tests means ensure tests always produce the same result and use assertions that explicitly state expected outcomes, not manual checks.. In practical terms, deterministic outcomes and explicit assertions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Timely tests are written before or alongside the production code, as in test-driven development. Writing tests first clarifies the public interface, forces you to think about edge cases, and keeps design focused on observable behavior. When tests are added after the fact, they often mirror implementation details and become brittle when the implementation changes. A short example: writing a test for a register_user function first makes you define what success should look like — a boolean result and a call to the repository — which keeps the service's interface minimal and testable. A misconception is that TDD adds overhead; in practice it reduces rework by catching design issues early. The takeaway is to treat tests as part of design: when possible, create a failing test that describes the expected behavior, implement the minimal code to pass it, and then refactor both code and tests together. Another misconception is that setting up everything in fixtures hides complexity; move setup into Arrange when it is specific to a single test. The takeaway: structure tests explicitly with AAA and keep each test focused on a single behavior. What would you extract into Arrange for a complex scenario?
